name: Brilliantine

card.summary: A perfumed, oil-based hair dressing that gives hair a smooth, glossy, slicked-back finish with little hold.
card.note: Oily hair products have been linked to acne-type eruptions on the face and rare contact allergy.

quick.overview:
Brilliantine is a perfumed oily liquid or cream for grooming hair, beards and moustaches. It gives a glossy, neat, slicked-back look and makes hair more manageable.

It was created by French perfumer Edouard Pinaud and shown at the 1900 Paris Exposition. Dermatology literature from the 1940s onward records acne-like eruptions from some brilliantines.
quick.how: Applied to wet or dry hair, brilliantine is used for sheen and smoothness rather than firm hold, often for pompadours and slicked styles. Vintage-style grooming fans still use it.
quick.risks: Old French dermatology reports describe oil acne (comedones and pimples) from brilliantine, and a case report describes allergic contact dermatitis. Reviews list brilliantine among causes of cosmetic-induced acne.

lead: Brilliantine is a perfumed, coloured oily liquid used to soften hair and give a glossy, well-groomed look to hair, beards and moustaches.[1][2] Its name comes from the French brillant, 'shining'.[2]

Édouard Pinaud is credited with creating it around 1900 and it was presented at the 1900 Exposition Universelle in Paris.[2][3] Its popularity peaked in the early twentieth century with slicked-back styles; Brylcreem, launched in 1928, offered a lighter cream version.[3] Modern gels and waxes reduced its use, but it remains a niche product for vintage-inspired grooming.[3]

Dermatology literature records acne-like skin reactions from oily hair dressings. French articles from 1945-1946 describe acneiform eruptions and facial oiliness caused by brilliantine,[5][6][7] and a 1991 case report describes allergic contact dermatitis.[8] A review on induced acne lists brilliantine acne among forms of cosmetic acne.[4]

chain: Hair lies smooth and reflects light
angle.text: Brilliantine adds shine and smoothness, letting hair be combed into a polished style with little stiffness.

paras: Typically made of oils such as mineral or almond oil with fragrance, brilliantine is used for gloss and manageability without strong hold.[3] Wikipedia describes it simply as a perfumed and coloured oily liquid.[2]

Macassar oil, marketed by Alexander Rowland from 1814, is a precursor.[3] Pinaud's brilliantine appeared at the 1900 Paris exposition; the Klotz family acquired the house in 1908 and expanded sales to the US.[3] It was popular from the 1920s to the 1940s alongside Hollywood slicked styles.[3]

Several French papers from 1945-46 report acneiform eruptions and oil comedones from a newly produced brilliantine.[5][6][7] A 2002 French review includes brilliantine acne among induced acne forms.[4] A case report describes allergic contact dermatitis.[8]
No controlled trials of brilliantine have been published. Published work consists of mid-twentieth-century case series and a case report of adverse skin reactions.[5][6][7][8]
